final_answer:
The assistant identifies that the sunk cost fallacy is a cognitive bias where individuals continue investing in a decision based on prior investments, even when it is no longer rational. This occurs because people emotionally weigh past expenditures, despite those costs being unrecoverable and irrelevant to future outcomes. The assistant selects three domains—business, personal relationships, and public policy—to provide varied examples.  

In business, a company might persist in funding a failing product development project because it has already spent millions, even though market analysis indicates the product has no viable future. The fallacy arises when the company ignores future costs and potential profits, instead clinging to the belief that “we’ve already invested so much.” A rational decision would involve cutting losses and redirecting resources.  

In personal relationships, an individual might stay in an unhealthy or unfulfilling marriage due to years of effort, time, or emotional investment, even though the relationship is clearly detrimental. The fallacy manifests when the person justifies staying because “I’ve already put so much into this,” rather than evaluating whether future happiness is possible. A rational choice would prioritize future well-being over past commitment.  

In public policy, a government might continue funding a costly infrastructure project that is clearly over budget and inefficient simply because it was initially approved by a previous administration. The fallacy occurs when officials prioritize avoiding “wasted” past spending over assessing whether the project will serve public needs effectively in the future. A rational approach would involve terminating the project and reallocating funds to alternatives with clearer benefits.  

The assistant concludes that each example illustrates how sunk costs distort decisions by conflating past irrecoverable investments with future value, while a rational framework focuses on incremental future costs and benefits.
